question: to the Commission Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left) Subject:

Throughout Europe, records for high temperatures are being broken time and again, and many people are feeling the severe effects of the heat. It is a particular problem for those who have to work in the heat. Figures from the European Trade Union Confederation show that the number of deaths in European workplaces is rising in line with the increase in temperatures. Accidents at work increase by 7% when the temperature exceeds 30 degrees and by 15% at temperatures over 38 degrees. The Commission has adopted a ‘vision zero’ approach to workrelated deaths. This is a central plank of the EU’s strategic framework on health and safety at work for 2021-2027, which aims to eliminate fatal accidents at work in the EU. 1.
How is the Commission’s work on vision zero affected by the fact that more people are now dying at work in these hotter conditions?
What specific measures is the Commission taking to ensure that Member States achieve vision zero now that deaths are on the increase with extreme temperatures of over 38 degrees?

This is not a short-term problem: it will continue to get worse as greenhouse gas emissions change our climate. What is the Commission doing to ensure that Member States make efforts not only to cut emissions but also to mitigate the consequences of a hotter climate?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The data collection ‘The European Statistics on Accidents at Work’1 compiled by Eurostat, shows that the incidence rate of fatal work accidents in the EU-27 fell by nearly 30% between 2010 and 20232, the latest year for which data are currently available, although several of the final years of this period were among the hottest on record in Europe3. The EU has strong rules for addressing occupational safety and health (OSH) risks. In particular, the Framework Directive on Safety and Health at Work requires employers to assess and address all OSH risks, including heat-related risks4. In addition, the Commission and the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work provide guidance and practical tools to support the implementation of EU OSH legislation, including measures to address heat at work5.All policy activities of the Commission in the field of OSH contribute to the objective of zero work-related deaths, as set out in the EU Strategic Framework on Health and Safety at Work 2021–20276. The EU has put in place an ambitious legislative framework to reduce its net greenhouse gas emissions7. In addition, the Commission is currently developing a new European framework to strengthen climate resilience and preparedness across all levels of government and policy areas, which it expects to adopt during the 4th quarter of 2026. Strategy8 proposes preparedness for all hazards. For heatwaves, this includes early warning, prevention, resilient infrastructure, healthcare preparedness and community action. The Commission is exploring further heatwave preparedness actions to complement Member State efforts.
